cap1.abertura.p2: The war ended five years ago. The city still bears its scars, but the trams are running through the streets again, and in the parks the old men are back at their chessboards until dark.
cap1.abertura.p3: In the newspapers and on the radio, chess is serious business. The world champion is one of ours, Mikhail Botvinnik, and he has just been handed a challenger: the young master David Bronstein.
cap1.abertura.p4: You are thirteen. Your grandfather taught you the moves on a wooden board that still sits in your room.
cap1.abertura.p5: You don't know it yet, but this is where a road begins, one that could lead all the way to the throne.
cap1.quarto.livro.texto:
An old book of your grandfather's, its cover long gone, full of Capablanca's games. Grandfather used to say the Cuban played chess the way other people breathe: without any effort at all.

In the margins, his tiny handwriting insists, page after page: "Simplify. Always simplify."
cap1.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The wooden board where you learned the moves. The white knight has had a chipped ear ever since it fell off the table.

For weeks you have only played against yourself, turning the board around after every move. It is time to find real opponents.
cap1.fechamento.aprovado:
The sun has already set when Mr. Ozols puts the pieces back in their wooden box.

"You are not a beginner anymore," he says, without looking up from the box. "Tomorrow afternoon, wait for me here. I'll take you to a place where boys like you learn properly."
cap1.fechamento.reprovado:
Night falls over the park. The old men pack up their pieces and walk home arguing about the day's games.

Nobody is born knowing. Tomorrow they will be here again — and so will you.
adv.peteris.apresentacao: Eleven years old, pockets full of lost pieces. Plays fast and loves bringing his queen out early.
adv.grisha.apresentacao: A retired railwayman. Smokes a pipe, tells war stories and never turns down a queen trade.
adv.ozols.apresentacao: A watchmaker in his early sixties. The "king of the park": nobody remembers seeing him lose twice in a row.
dlg.peteris.inicio: Hey! Are you new here? I'm Pēteris. Old Ozols says I play too fast, but he's the one who plays too slow. Want a game? I'll take Black, it's my lucky colour.
dlg.peteris.depois_vitoria: Oh no! I was going to mate you next move… Almost. I'll get my revenge tomorrow, you'll see.
dlg.peteris.depois_derrota: See? Bringing the queen out early works! Tell Ozols, he never believes me.
dlg.peteris.depois_empate: A draw? Boring. Nobody wins anything with a draw.
dlg.grisha.inicio: Sit down, lad. Thirty years on the rails at Riga station, and now this is my train: sixty-four squares. I'll take White, if you don't mind. Old men have their habits.
dlg.grisha.guerra: During the war we played with pieces made of dried bread, on a board scratched into the lid of a box. When hunger got bad, a pawn that left the board didn't go back in the box… Well, enough sad stories. Shall we play?
dlg.grisha.depois_vitoria: Hmm. You calculate better than you look. A boy like you shouldn't stay in the park forever.
dlg.grisha.depois_derrota: Don't look so glum. I lost the first game of my life to my little brother, and he never let me forget it.
dlg.grisha.depois_empate: A fair draw. Like two engine drivers on the same track who both brake in time.
dlg.ozols.inicio: Hm. The new boy. I've heard about you. Here in the park I'm the last step, you understand? Whoever beats me can go and look for better opponents. Want to try?
dlg.ozols.depois_vitoria: … Well played. It's been a long time since anyone caught me like that. You need stronger people than this old man.
dlg.ozols.depois_derrota: Don't lose heart. I've been repairing watches for forty years: everything worth anything works with patience. Chess too.
dlg.ozols.depois_empate: A draw with old Ozols. That's not nothing, boy. That's not nothing.
dlg.marta.inicio: Good afternoon! Come to fetch your father's paper? Or are you here for the old chess players? They stay until dark.
dlg.marta.op_melhor: Who's the best in the park?
dlg.marta.novidades: It was in the paper: two of ours, Bronstein and Boleslavsky, tied for first in Budapest and had to play a whole match just to decide who challenges Botvinnik. Bronstein won. Soviet against Soviet for the chance to face another Soviet — imagine that!
dlg.marta.melhor: Mr. Ozols, the watchmaker. They say he once drew with a real master, but nobody saw it. He never denied it, either.
not.n1950_budapeste.titulo: A tie at the top in Budapest
not.n1950_budapeste.texto: The Candidates Tournament in Budapest ended with two Soviet players sharing first place: David Bronstein and Isaac Boleslavsky. One of them will be Mikhail Botvinnik's challenger.
not.n1950_desempate.texto: In the play-off match held in Moscow, David Bronstein beat Isaac Boleslavsky 7½–6½ — after the twelve scheduled games ended 6–6 — and won the right to play Mikhail Botvinnik for the world title.
not.n1950_titulos.texto: For the first time, the International Chess Federation has officially awarded the title of grandmaster, to 27 players. Eleven are Soviets — among them champion Botvinnik, Smyslov, Keres, Bronstein, Boleslavsky and the veteran Levenfish.
not.n1950_mezgailis.texto: Voldemārs Mežgailis has won the 1950 Latvian championship, repeating his title of 1944. The women's champion is Milda Lauberte.
not.n1950_final_urss.titulo: The Soviet championship final begins in Moscow
not.n1950_final_urss.texto: Eighteen masters are contesting the final of the 18th USSR Championship. Keres, Boleslavsky and Smyslov were seeded straight in; the rest came through the quarter-finals and semi-finals, including the one in Tartu, just over the border in Estonia.
dlg.marta.op_garoto: Are there any good boys here in Riga?
dlg.marta.garoto: There's Doctor Tal's son, Misha. He won the Latvian junior championship this year! They say that when he was even smaller he knocked on Botvinnik's door — the champion was on holiday here in Riga — asking for a game. The champion's wife told him he was asleep…
cap2.abertura.p2: Since that afternoon in the park, Mr. Ozols has treated you differently. He decided that somebody had to take care of your chess, and that somebody would not be a watchmaker.
cap2.abertura.p3: In Moscow, the world title match has just ended: twelve all. Bronstein was a point ahead with two games to go, but Botvinnik is still world champion. On the park benches, nobody talks about anything else.
cap2.abertura.p4: This afternoon, Mr. Ozols is taking you to the Pioneers' Palace, in the old Riga Castle. Inside, at the end of a corridor, there is a door with a sign on it: Chess Section.
cap2.quarto.saida: Go to the Palace with Mr. Ozols
cap2.quarto.livro.texto:
The notebook Mr. Ozols gave you the day after the park challenge. On the first page, in his careful hand: "A game you don't write down is lost. A game you write down teaches you twice."

You wrote down the three park games from memory. Some of the moves still make you blush.
cap2.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
For weeks, grandfather's board has not rested. You replayed the Moscow match games as they came out in the magazine, one by one, trying to understand how Bronstein, a point ahead, let the title slip away at the end.

Today it stays at home. Today you will play on a board that isn't yours.
cap2.local.vitrine.cabecalho: The display case in the corridor
cap2.local.vitrine.texto:
Small cups, pennants from junior tournaments, photographs of teams standing in a row, all in white shirts. A typed card reminds visitors that the Palace has occupied the north wing of the castle since 1941 and turns ten this year.

You catch yourself imagining your name in one of those photographs.
cap2.fechamento.aprovado:
Mr. Krūzkops looks at the board for a long time, writes something in his notebook and says only: "Tuesdays and Thursdays, at four. Don't be late."

In the corridor, Misha catches up with you. "He said Tuesdays and Thursdays? Then you're in. He never says more than that."
cap2.fechamento.reprovado: Mr. Krūzkops wipes the board clean with the sleeve of his jacket. "Come back next week, there will be another tournament. A lost tournament teaches you something too. Sometimes it teaches you more."
adv.valdis.apresentacao: Thirteen, always the first to arrive. Plays fast when he is nervous, and he is always nervous.
adv.ilze.apresentacao: Fourteen, the only girl in the group, and the one who makes the fewest mistakes. Writes down her games in flawless handwriting.
adv.boris.apresentacao: Fifteen, the oldest in the group. Loves gambits: gives up a pawn early and spends the game trying to prove it was worth it.
adv.gipslis.apresentacao: Fourteen. He learned chess right here at the Palace only two years ago, and he is already one of the strongest in the group.
dlg.kruzkops.inicio: So you're the boy from the park. Mr. Ozols says you gave him a hard time. In the mornings I teach English; in the afternoons, chess. Our group's internal tournament starts today: five players, everyone plays everyone. It's the quickest way for me to see how you play.
dlg.kruzkops.regras: One game per round, with a clock: two hours each. You play Valdis, Ilze, Boris and Aivars, in that order; in the last round you have a bye. The results go on the board on the wall. Whoever scores two and a half points joins the group.
dlg.kruzkops.ativo: Active chess. Nobody here runs away from a complicated position. A quiet position teaches you little; whoever learns to think in the middle of the fire will play calmly anywhere.
dlg.tal.inicio: Are you the new one? I'm Misha. Do you know how I ended up here? I came for the drama group. Then, in the corridor, I saw a door with a sign saying "Chess Section"… I went in, and I never came out.
dlg.tal.op_porta: Is it true you knocked on Botvinnik's door?
dlg.tal.porta: I did! He was on holiday here in Riga, after winning the title. I wanted to play a game with the world champion. His wife opened the door and said he was asleep, and that he was taking a rest from chess. A rest from chess! To this day I don't understand what that means.
dlg.tal.op_torneio: Are you playing the group tournament?
dlg.tal.torneio: Not this one. I already play in the adult tournaments, and I get beaten by real masters, which teaches you more. But I'll be watching your games. One piece of advice: Boris always gives up a pawn. Sometimes it's worth taking it.
dlg.valdis.inicio: Hi… you're the one from the park, right? I play fast, don't mind me. When I get nervous, my hand moves by itself.
dlg.valdis.depois_vitoria: I knew my hand would move before I thought. I always do that. Good game.
dlg.valdis.depois_derrota: I won? I won! Sorry… it's just that I almost never beat anyone new.
dlg.valdis.depois_empate: A draw. For me, that's almost a win.
dlg.ilze.inicio: Ilze. I write everything down, so there's no point arguing about a move afterwards. Good luck in your round.
dlg.ilze.depois_vitoria: You were better today. But it's all written down: next time, I'll know where you go wrong.
dlg.ilze.depois_derrota: I wrote down your game too. Do you want to see where it turned? You don't have to answer now.
dlg.ilze.depois_empate: A fair draw. I'll study the endgame at home.
dlg.boris.inicio: Boris. Do you play book openings? I don't. Books are for people who are scared. I give up a pawn on move three and see what happens.
dlg.boris.depois_vitoria: The pawn wasn't worth it today. But one day it will be, you'll see.
dlg.boris.depois_derrota: See? The pawn always comes back with interest.
dlg.boris.depois_empate: A draw? Nobody gives up a pawn to make a draw. What a waste.
dlg.gipslis.inicio: Aivars. I only learned chess two years ago, right here. So don't be alarmed if I think a lot: I'm still learning.
dlg.gipslis.depois_vitoria: Good game. I took too long in the middlegame and the clock made me pay. I'll remember that.
dlg.gipslis.depois_derrota: Thanks for the game. You played the opening well; the trouble came later.
dlg.gipslis.depois_empate: A draw. It was a serious game. I liked it.
not.n1951_palacio_10_anos.texto: The Republic's Pioneers' Palace, housed since 1941 in the north wing of the old Riga Castle, celebrates its first decade. The Palace's clubs now cover 44 fields of activity, among them the chess section, with nearly a thousand pupils in all.
not.n1951_match_comeca.titulo: World title match begins in Moscow
not.n1951_match_comeca.texto: Mikhail Botvinnik defends his world championship title against David Bronstein, winner of the Candidates Tournament. The match is over 24 games; if it ends twelve all, the champion keeps the title.
not.n1951_match_fim.texto: The Moscow match has ended twelve all. Bronstein won the 21st and 22nd games and led by a point with two to go; Botvinnik won the 23rd, the 24th was drawn, and the title stays with the champion.
cap1.fechamento.tentar: Come back to the park tomorrow
cap3.abertura.p2: For more than a year you have spent Tuesdays and Thursdays at the Palace. Mr Krūzkops hardly praises anyone, but last month he stopped behind your chair, watched a whole game and said only: "It's time."
cap3.abertura.p3: Time for what, you found out the next day: he had entered you in the semi-final of the Riga championship. A grown-ups' tournament. Engineers, army men, university students, people who have played chess since before you were born.
cap3.abertura.p4: You are fifteen. It is the first time someone will look across the board and see you as an opponent, not as the boy from the Palace.
cap3.quarto.livro.texto:
The notebook Mr Ozols gave you is almost full. The games from the class tournament, the ones from the Palace, the ones you played against Misha in the breaks and lost nearly every time.

On the last blank page you wrote the name of tomorrow's tournament, and under it, in small letters, a question: "Will they let me really play?"
cap3.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The knight with the chipped ear is still in its place. Mr Krūzkops warned you: in grown-up tournaments, a game that isn't finished in the session is adjourned. The move goes into an envelope, and the analysis goes on at home, at night.

If that happens, this is the board where you'll spend the night.
cap3.local.aviso.texto:
Typed, with a crooked stamp at the foot of the page:

1. Two and a half hours for each player for the first forty moves.
2. After the fortieth move the session ends. The player whose turn it is writes down his move and hands it to the arbiter in a sealed envelope.
3. An adjourned game is resumed the next morning, with one more hour for each player.
4. Talking near the tables and analysing in the hall are forbidden.

Someone has added in pencil underneath: "and smoking only in the corridor". Nobody obeys.
cap3.local.jornal.cabecalho: A newspaper left on a chair
cap3.fechamento.aprovado:
The arbiter writes the last result on the table and draws a line under your name. Someone behind you says, quietly: "the boy from the Palace". It doesn't sound like a joke any more.

On the way out, Mr Krūzkops shakes your hand, the way you shake a grown man's hand. "Next year, the final of the Latvian championship. Misha will be there too. Get ready."
cap3.fechamento.reprovado:
The arbiter rubs out your last result and chalks it in again, harder, as if he had to be sure.

Mr Ozols is waiting at the door, hat in hand. "Grown-ups blunder just like children, they only take longer. You saw it. At the next semi-final, they'll be the ones afraid of the boy."
adv.kalnins.apresentacao: An engineer at a radio factory, in his early thirties. He plays the way he builds a circuit: slowly, part by part, never skipping a step.
adv.sokolov.apresentacao: A reserve officer of fifty, always in his tunic. He attacks the king as if taking a hill, and he doesn't like to retreat.
adv.zenta.apresentacao: Twenty, a mathematics student at the university. She works out variations on café napkins and almost never gets into time trouble.
adv.zilber.apresentacao: Nineteen, born in Riga, the strongest in the group. This year he beat Misha Tal. He plays fast, smiles little and forgives nothing.
dlg.ozols_clube.inicio: I closed the shop early today. The park boy's first grown-up tournament: an old man doesn't miss that. I'll be over in the corner, quiet. I promise not to give advice.
dlg.ozols_clube.nervoso: Of course you are. So would I be. A watchmaker's advice: look at the clock only after you've moved, never before. Whoever plays looking at the clock plays in a hurry, and hurry is the one thing I've never managed to fix in anyone.
dlg.ozols_clube.op_adultos: What are grown-ups like at the board?
dlg.ozols_clube.adultos: Just like you, boy. Only they get tired. By the fifth hour the engineer forgets his factory, the major forgets the war, and everybody blunders. Whoever is still in one piece at the end of the session wins. And you are fifteen.
dlg.tal_clube.inicio: You're here! Krūzkops told me. I'm in the other group of this semi-final, so today I only came to watch. Well, to watch and suffer: Zilber ended up in your group. He beat me this year, did you know?
dlg.tal_clube.op_adiada: Have you ever had a game adjourned?
dlg.tal_clube.adiada: Once, in a Palace tournament, when I was still small. The game was adjourned and I thought the position was lost, I almost resigned. That night I dreamt of an idea. In the morning, at the resumption, it took me ten minutes to find the real move, and I won. Ever since, when one of my games is adjourned, I go to bed early.
dlg.tal_clube.letonia: Seventh place. I lost the first game to an opening trap, imagine, me, in a trap. And Zilber beat me. But I beat Pasman, who was the champion. Next year will be different. Next year you'll be there too.
dlg.arbitro.inicio: You're Krūzkops's boy? Welcome. Here the rules are the same for everyone, fifteen or fifty. If you have a question, ask it now: during the game, I don't talk.
dlg.arbitro.op_envelope: How does the sealed move work?
dlg.arbitro.envelope: After the fortieth move, the session ends. Whoever has the move doesn't play it on the board: he writes it on a slip of paper, shows nobody, and hands it to me. I seal the envelope, you both sign across the flap, and it sleeps in my drawer. In the morning I open it, make the move, and the clock starts again.
dlg.arbitro.op_tempo: How much time does each player have?
dlg.arbitro.tempo: Two and a half hours for the first forty moves. At the resumption, one more hour. If your flag falls before that, the game is lost, and there's no point complaining: the clocks are checked every day.
dlg.kalnins.inicio: Kalniņš, pleased to meet you. Engineer. Don't be alarmed by how calm I am: I spend my days building radios, and a radio built in a hurry doesn't play. Chess is the same.
dlg.kalnins.depois_vitoria: Hm. You soldered everything in the right place. Well done, young man.
dlg.kalnins.depois_derrota: Don't take it hard. At the factory we say: every apprentice's first radio crackles. The second one plays.
dlg.kalnins.depois_empate: A draw. A balanced circuit. I liked it.
dlg.sokolov.inicio: Major Sokolov, reserve. So you're the boy. Very well: at the board there's no age, only position. Don't expect me to go easy.
dlg.sokolov.op_guerra: Where did you learn to play?
dlg.sokolov.guerra: In a field hospital, in 1943, with my leg in plaster and a cardboard board. The doctor played better than he operated, thank God for me. I walked out of there playing. Shall we play our round?
dlg.sokolov.depois_vitoria: I retreated too late. I always retreat too late. Well played, soldier.
dlg.sokolov.depois_derrota: That's how attacking is: whoever hesitates loses. You hesitated. Next time, don't.
dlg.zenta.inicio: Zenta. Mathematics, third year. You must be wondering what a girl is doing here. The same thing as you: playing.
dlg.zenta.matematica: It helps you count. It doesn't help you choose. I can calculate a variation to the end; the trouble is that after three good variations I still have to play just one. No professor teaches that.
dlg.zenta.depois_vitoria: You chose better than I did. I'll think about it on the way home.
dlg.zenta.depois_derrota: I calculated it to the end. Sorry, it was a closed sum.
dlg.zenta.depois_empate: A draw. Equality is a beautiful result, you know. In mathematics, at least.
dlg.zilber.inicio: Zilber. I've heard of you, the other one from the Palace. Good. I beat Misha this year; let's see if his friend plays any better.
dlg.zilber.misha: He wanted to complicate things, so I let him. Whoever complicates too much sometimes gets tangled up on his own. Will it be different with you? Show me.
dlg.zilber.depois_vitoria: … Well played. I don't like losing, but I know when the other man played better. See you in the final.
dlg.zilber.depois_derrota: You're good. But you need about a hundred more games like this one.
dlg.zilber.depois_empate: A draw. Against me, this year, that's no small thing. Ask Misha.
not.n1952_helsinque.titulo: On its debut, the USSR wins the Olympiad
not.n1952_helsinque.texto: At the first chess Olympiad it has ever entered, in Helsinki, the Soviet team took the gold: 21 points, ahead of Argentina (19½) and Yugoslavia (19), among 25 countries. Keres, Smyslov, Bronstein, Geller, Boleslavsky and Kotov played. Smyslov and Bronstein won prizes for their boards.
not.n1952_interzonal.titulo: Kotov wins the Interzonal without losing a game
not.n1952_interzonal.texto: The Interzonal tournament has ended in Sweden, near Stockholm: Alexander Kotov won with 16½ points out of 21, without a single defeat. Taimanov and Petrosian shared second place with 13½, and Geller was fourth. The leaders go on to the Candidates tournament, which decides Botvinnik's next challenger.
not.n1952_letonia.texto: The Latvian championship ended in Riga in March: the title went to Jānis Kļaviņš. Among the finalists were the masters Koblencs and Solmanis, last year's champion Pasman, and two young players from the Pioneers' Palace: Israel Zilber, in fourth place, and fifteen-year-old Mikhail Tal, seventh. In the women's event, Milda Lauberte won again.
not.n1952_semifinal_riga.titulo: Riga hosts a semi-final of the Soviet championship
not.n1952_semifinal_riga.texto: Eighteen masters played one of the semi-finals of the USSR championship in Riga in May and June. Ilya Kan won with 12½ points; Tolush, second, did not lose a single game. The home players struggled against the visiting masters: Kļaviņš scored 7½, Koblencs 7 and Pasman 5.
not.n1952_jogos_helsinque.texto: For the first time the Soviet Union went to the Olympic Games, in Helsinki, and came home with 71 medals, 22 of them gold, second only to the United States. In basketball the Soviet team took silver; one of its players was eighteen-year-old Maigonis Valdmanis, born here in Riga.
